questions.q: Ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise together. This shows…
options: Correlation, not causation (a hot day drives both)
questions.explain: Two things moving together doesn't mean one causes the other — look for a common cause.

options: Looks impressive but doesn't guide a decision
questions.explain: If a metric goes up and you'd do nothing differently, it's vanity. Track metrics that change actions.

questions.q: One customer spent £1m; the rest spent £5. The average is misleading because of…
options: An outlier skewing the mean — use the median
questions.explain: Outliers drag the mean. The median often describes 'typical' far better.

questions.q: Before trusting a chart, you should first check…
options: The source, the time range, and the axis scale
questions.explain: Source, range and axis can flip the story. Always read them before you believe the shape.

questions.q: A good metric to act on is…
options: One tied to a goal, with a baseline to compare against
questions.explain: Goal-linked metrics with a baseline tell you whether you're actually improving.

questions.q: Your sample is 8 people, all from one team. The risk is…
options: It's not representative — conclusions may not generalise
Nothing, more data is always worse
questions.explain: A small, skewed sample can mislead. Make sure it represents the population you care about.
